The only person who would be likely to know of her would be Joseph D. Sharon, of Winchester, xxx I heard of her marriage from them.”

Name: Henrietta Bacon
entry_text: Letter from Mr. Joseph D. Sharon, Winchester, Mass. January 1889: “After leaving the School Henrietta lived at several places, and was finally married to a young man named Covell. He went to the war, and was killed in the Battle of the Wilderness. She then came to my house, and gave birth to a boy, who is now … grown up to be a young man, & a very nice man. He is an apothecary's clerk in the drug-store in this town. After a time Henrietta married again. Her husband is Henry S. Brookings, a house-painter, and they have one little girl living, having buried one. Henrietta always was a good girl, and has grown up to be a fine woman: she is a member of the Baptist Church. She lives in this town, her husband owning the house they live in.” Mr Sharon says later that Henrietta does not like any allusion to her having been in the school.

Name: Monica Butler
entry_text: Ran away from Mr. Goodrich's family. Mr. G. having died & the family under the charge of a young daughter. She had not been paid the sum agreed upon for more than a year, & in going carried away with her, clothes belonging to the daughters of the family. It is supposed she went to her Father. She has not come to claim the money still in Mrs Parker's hands, & being so nearly 18, thought best to leave her.

Name: Monica Butler
entry_text: Learned that Monica Butler married, & is now Mrs. Edward J. Barry, living at 48. Beach Street. According to report she is a woman of bad character, having been many times before the Municipal Court for keeping a bad house. In spite of this, she was kind to her sister's children, (See p. 35) & gave them a home, although a bad one. She has children of her own. (pasted newspaper clipping, dated in pencil “1897”; printed text:) MONICA BARRY CAUGHT AT LAST. Has Eluded Police of This City Many Times, but Failed at the Trick Last Night. — The clipping reports that Monica Barry, age 45, long sought by police, was arrested after being found hidden beneath a sofa at a house on Tyler street; that she was wanted on a default warrant from the superior criminal court; and that she had earlier been charged in connection with a disorderly house on Prospect street, convicted in the lower court, appealed, and disappeared before sentencing.

Name: Sally Aberbach

Name: Sally Aberbach
entry_text: It had been represented to the Board that Sally Aberbock, a girl bound to Mr. and Mrs. Kendrick, was in the “House of reformation for Juvenile Offenders.” That the Committee had enquired into the causes of this procedure and found that the charge had been that of disobedience. They had taken all the measures which seemed to them expedient, and requested the Secretary to notify Mr. Kendrick to attend this meeting. He accordingly came with his wife. They made many complaints of the girl, and professed that knowing no other means to rid themselves of a troublesome child they had resorted to this. It was considered by the Board as a very improper measure, and a violation of the Indenture. But as she was under the care of an excellent woman, and the Directors of the House had promised that she should remain there till the further decision of the Board, it was thought best to endeavor to procure a suitable place for her, and leave the result till the next meeting.

Name: Sally Aberbach
entry_text: On the urgent solicitations of the brother and sisters of Sally Aberbock, an application signed by the Members of the Board had been made to the Directors of House of Reformation for Juvenile Offenders, requesting that the brother might be allowed to take her under his care on the supposition that she was to be under his immediate protection. The following answer was given. “The undersigned, Directors of the House of Reformation for Juvenile Offenders, received at their last Meeting the communication of the Board of Managers of the Female Asylum and immediately proceeded to take the necessary steps to comply with the request contained in it relative to the discharge of Sally Aberlock. The enquires they have consequently made have led them however to believe that the situation in which the girl would probably be placed, would be one of much exposure and moral danger. A child of her age and character at board, with no one to exercise any thing like constant supervision over her, and under the care of a brother, who however respectable and well disposed has hitherto given her very little of his personal attention, and is not now in a situation enable him to do so will be in great danger of going astray. And although a place might be found for her which would be more eligible the Directors beg leave respectfully to suggest whether it would not be safer that she should be under their control in the intrim and that her future situation should be determined by themselves rather than by her brother. They have learnt from the brother who being a single man, cannot give her the protection which is so desirable, that this course would be in conformity with his own wishes on the subject, and they have therefore concluded to retain the girl under their charge till they could ascertain the pleasure of the Managers of the Asylum. Very respectfully Moses Grant Saml. A. Eliot” In conformity with the directions of the Board the following reply was given. The Managers of the B.F. Asylum received at their meeting on Tuesday last the communication of the Directors of the House of Reformation for Juvenile Offenders respecting Sally Aberbock. The duly appreciate the motives of the Directors in withholding the girl from her relatives and willingly acquisse in their decision believing that they are more fully acquainted with the comparative advantages of her remaining in her present situation till another can be provided, than those can be who, knowing little of the regulations of the establishment, have considered it only as a place of public punishment and consequent disgrace. The Managers will endeaver to obtain for the girl a suitable place. If any application should be made at the House which the Directors approve, the Managers will be much obliged to have notice of it, and they request permission that the Indentures may be given from them rather than from the Directors. The Managers would again express their grateful sense of the interest the Directors have taken in this painful subject, and offer the assurance of their “respectful consideration.”

entry_text: The Committee reported that Agnes Alexander, who had been living on trial with Mrs. Jephson in Newton, had been returned to the Asylum during the month, Mrs. Jephson having found it impossible to bear with her any longer. Name: Elizabeth Barnfield
entry_text: Doctor Eaton presented Mary & Elizabeth Barnfield, twin sisters, Four years old under the following circumstances. Their parents brought the family from England last July, in the hope of surporting them by the labour as a stone-mason. But in the Autumn his eyes became so much affected as to prevent his working at the trade and his wife was at length obliged, though very unwillingly to solicit charity. For this purpose she went out during the recent bad weather and on her return was attacked with fever on the brain of which she died on Saturday last, leaving Nine children of whom the eldest is only Eleven years and the youngest our Months. Voted: That Mary and Elizabeth Barnfield be admitted.

Name: Elizabeth Barnfield
entry_text: The father of Mary and Elizabeth Barnfield mentioned on the Record of February 1833 being in no better situation to support his family solicited admission for his next daughter Harriet now old enough to enter the Asylum Voted: That Harriet Barnfield be admitted.

Name: Sally Brintnall
entry_text: Mrs. May applied for the admission of two orphan children named Brintnall. Susan Stowell, Mary Baker, Cynthia Hayden, and the child of a Mrs. Nance were also proposed as very destitute claimants to the protection of this Society. As it was necessary to make a selection of the most necessitous from among these applicants it was directed that their names be recorded and further enquiry made into their respective situations.

Name: Sally Brintnall
entry_text: On examination of the claims of the several candidates for admission it was found that the two children named Brintnall were by the recent death of their father left in a very destitute and friendless situation. From their mother, a very abandoned woman, her had some years before been divorced. He again married, and has now left an impoverished widow who, having several children of her own to support, feels authorized and indeed compelled to decline taking charge of these friendless and peculiarly unfortunate orphans. Voted: That Sally and Mary Brintnall be admitted.

Name: Sally Brintnall
entry_text: Voted: That Sally Brintnall be bound to F.W. Mitchell and wife of Nantucket.

Name: Sally Brintnall
entry_text: Voted: That the request of James and Eliza Dalton for Mary Brintnall to be placed under their care be granted.

Name: Sally Brintnall
entry_text: The Secretary communicated a letter from Mrs. Mitchell of Nantucket, stating that S. Brintnall still continued in her service on wages, and would continue to do so at present.

Name: Sally Brintnall
entry_text: The Secretary presented a list of Ten children who had become free within the last year. Among these are…Mary Brintnall…to those holding their Indentures the usuall circulars had been sent.

Name: Sally Brintnall
entry_text: Miss Huse presented herself with Catharine Courtney and the Misses Daltons with Mary Brintnall. Of both these girls very excellent characters were given and both were to remain employed in the families in which they had served their apprenticeships.

Name: Mary Brintnall
entry_text: Mrs. May applied for the admission of two orphan children named Brintnall. Susan Stowell, Mary Baker, Cynthia Hayden, and the child of a Mrs. Nance were also proposed as very destitute claimants to the protection of this Society. As it was necessary to make a selection of the most necessitous from among these applicants it was directed that their names be recorded and further enquiry made into their respective situations.

Name: Mary Brintnall
entry_text: On examination of the claims of the several candidates for admission it was found that the two children named Brintnall were by the recent death of their father left in a very destitute and friendless situation. From their mother, a very abandoned woman, her had some years before been divorced. He again married, and has now left an impoverished widow who, having several children of her own to support, feels authorized and indeed compelled to decline taking charge of these friendless and peculiarly unfortunate orphans. Voted: That Sally and Mary Brintnall be admitted.

Name: Mary Brintnall
entry_text: Voted: That Sally Brintnall be bound to F.W. Mitchell and wife of Nantucket.

Name: Mary Brintnall
entry_text: Voted: That the request of James and Eliza Dalton for Mary Brintnall to be placed under their care be granted.

Name: Ella Doherty
entry_text: [annual meeting] the rite of baptism was administered to the children whose names follow: Ella Doherty.

Name: Ella Doherty
entry_text: Miss Lamb on the part of the Committee reported that three children had been admitted since the last meeting. … The other little child was brought to the Asylum by her aunt Mrs. Gibbs. She had no father; her mother has been a capable woman, but had now given herself up to habits of intoxication, and had abandoned her child. These circumstances having been heard, it was Voted: That the act of the Committee in admitting … Ella Doherty is approved by the Board.

Name: Ella Doherty
entry_text: Two applications for girls had been made. Mr. and Mrs. Woodward of North Cambridge wished to take Ella Doherty and Miss Fettyplace of East Boston to take Ella White. The former place was recommended by Rev. Mr. Holland and the latter was known to be a good place. Neither of the applicants however appeared at the meeting. It was Voted: That they have permission to take the two girls if they come for them during the month.

Name: Ella Doherty
entry_text: That Mr. and Mrs. E.G. Chase of Needham had made application for Ella Doherty and Mr. and Mrs. John H. Noble of Somerville desired to take Mary Ann Cox. Excellent recommendations of both families having been obtained it was Voted: That both these requests be granted.

Name: Ella Doherty
entry_text: Complaints were made of Ella Doherty and Mary Jane Armstrong by Mr. Chase and Mr. Carnes. It was decided to permit those gentleman to provide other places for the girls.

Name: Ella Doherty
entry_text: Mr. Chase also desired to return Ella Doherty to the Asylum, as his wife was now in Europe and there was no one with any proper authority over the child. As Mr. Chase had never signed his Indenture it was useless for the Board to oppose this step.

Name: Ella Doherty
entry_text: The Committee also stated that Ella Doherty had run away from her place and had gone to her Mother, from whom it would be difficult to remove her, as she had never signed the books surrendering the child.

Name: Catherine Harrington
entry_text: The Committee reported that three children had been admitted since the last meeting, Catharine Harrington, and Elizabeth and Anna Maria Sullivan. The first was offered for admission by her father. The mother had died leaving three children; the father was a man of intemperate habits, his health was poor, and he was not able to pay the board of the child; the older sister a girl of thirteen was at service where she could remain if this little girl could be provided for. This case was presented to the Board by Mrs. McGregor. Voted: That the Board approve the act of the Committee in admitting these children.

Name: Catherine Harrington
entry_text: Mrs. McGregor stated that Mr. Buckley, a relative of Catharine Harrington and a very respectable mechanic might very probably soon go to Ireland. He would in that case be willing to take Catharine with him and place her in charge of her relations there. Her Aunt Kate Buckley would sign the Indentures. The Managers were satisfied that this arrangement should be made.

Name: Catherine Harrington
entry_text: An excellent offer of a place for Catherine Harrington in Gilmanton N.H. was received. Mrs. Badger was well known to Mrs. Bartlett, she lived on a farm with her son, and the situation seemed such a favorable one that the Managers Voted: That after the September Meeting Catharine Harrington be bound to Mrs. Badger.

Name: Catherine Harrington
entry_text: The Committee reported that Sarah Johnson had been gone on trial to live with Mrs. Oliver in Malden, instead of to Mrs. Welch. Mrs. Welch now made application for Catharine Harrington. The recommendations being of the most satisfactory character it was Voted: That Catharine Harrington be bound to Mr. and Mrs. Welsh.

Name: Catherine Harrington
entry_text: Complaints of Catharine Harrington had been made by Mrs. Welch, and she had been advised either to transfer her to some other person, or to put her into one of the Public Institutions.

Name: Catherine Harrington
entry_text: Mrs. Welch had found it impossible to keep Catharine Harrington and it was thought had placed her in the Lancaster State Reform School.

Name: Catherine Harrington
entry_text: The Committee reported … that Catharine Harrington had been sent to Lancaster according to the permission some time ago given to Mrs. Welch.

Name: Charlotte Amelia Adams
entry_text:
Miss Inches presented to the Board the case of a very destitute little girl named Charlotte
Amelia Adams, for whose admission application had been made. The child’s father died in England; the
mother married again leaving four little girls in the care of an older sister. The sister not liking the charge,
came to America bringing Charlotte with her and leaving the others behind. She now manifested little
interest in the child, and was besides supposed to be a very unfit guardian for her. The little girl was now
eleven years old, but was thought to have contracted no bad habits; her board had been paid for some time
by Mr. [Crosby] a machinist who had become interested in her, assisted by other friends. These
circumstances having been heard, it was unanimously
Voted: That this peculiarly destitute child be admitted.

Name: Charlotte Amelia Adams
entry_text:
[annual meeting] No child was admitted till March, when an interesting and peculiarly
destitute little girl became one of our family. Her father died in England, leaving a wife and five children.
His widow married again, but left her four younger children under the care of the eldest daughter, herself
quite a young girl. This older sister came to America, bringing our little Charlotte with her, while the rest
remained in England. The child’s life after she came to this country was not in all respects a happy one; she
was sick, and was for some time in the Massachusetts Hospital, where a great deal of interest was felt for
her, and much kindness shown to her. When she left the Hospital he board was paid by persons who has
become interested in her, for her sister had no means of supporting her. We were very glad to be able to
offer her here a safe and comfortable home.

Name: Charlotte Amelia Adams
entry_text: It was mentioned that Charlotte Adams was very ill with typhoid fever.

Name: Charlotte Amelia Adams
entry_text:
The Committee reported that Charlotte Adams had died a very few days after the last
meeting.

Name: Charlotte Amelia Adams
entry_text:
[annual meeting] At the October meeting two of the children were reported to be very sick,
one with typhoid fever, the other with rheumatism, which deprived her in great measure of the use of her
limbs. Before another month, the first, Charlotte Adams, had died. She had not been with us a year, but
her pleasant dispassion had made her much beloved. Her life of confinement might have been a hard one,
as her health had not for a long time been sound and almost all of her near relations are in England. She
had during her short life been thrown very much upon the care of strangers, but she always won from them
interest and kindness.

Name: Christina Elizabeth Adams
entry_text:
July 1814: Mrs. Prescott presented the request of Mrs. S.H. Walley on behalf of Christina Elizabeth
Adams, a destitute child whose father had died some years ago leaving a widow and two children; the
mother is now sick and unable to provide for their support solicites for one of them a place in the Asylum.
Voted: That Mrs. Prescott and Mrs. Thurston be a committee to examine more particularly respecting the
claims of this child, and that they have authority to cause her admission, after receiving the customary
certificate from a physician, should they find her a proper subject for this charity.

Name: Christina Elizabeth Adams
Hannah Holt Albert
entry_text: Hannah Holt Albert was also presented by her aunt, who stated that the mother of the child was dead; that the habits of her father were such as to render him unfit and unable to take care of her; that she had done this till her poverty rendered it longer impracticable; and that the father being now about embarking on a long voyage was anxious to gain this home for his child. Voted: That …Hannah H. Albert…be received.

Name: Hannah Holt Albert
entry_text: Voted: That the application of Mrs. Lovering for H.H. Albert be granted.

Name: Hannah Holt Albert
entry_text: Mrs. George Gay, to who Hannah H. Albert was bound in May 1828, came with the girl and one of her sisters, to represent that her sisters had found from a family record, that it also appeared from the date of her baptism at the Catholic Church that Hannah was two years older than the age registered, from the statement of the aunt who offered her for admission in October 1822, on the Asylum record; from which her Indenture was made. This Aunt is since dead; and the sisters claim Hannah’s freedom from the Indenture on the ground that she is in reality nearly Eighteen, though according to that instrument but sixteen years of age. Mrs. Gay said she was desirous of keeping the girl on the terms of the Indenture, but not to pay her wages as she did not think her capable of earning more than she now received. The statements of Mrs. Gay, the very youthful appearance of the girl and the wish she expressed to remain in her present situation induced the Managers to think, that though she could not be legally held, it would be better for her sisters to consent that she remain at least one year longer with Mrs. Gay. To advise was the only measure they felt authorized to take, as the Indenture given by them contained an error for which they were not responsible, the age having been received from the only source from which they could have supposed it necessary to obtain it. The sisters were requested to consider the subject and report their decision at the next meeting.

Name: Hannah Holt Albert
entry_text: The Secretary reported that the terms of Fourteen Indentures having expired during the past year she had gained of them all the information in her power. Viz. ...Hannah H. Albert. Mentioned on the Record of April 1834.

Name: Margaret Jane Alcorn
entry_text: Mrs. Pickman on the part of the Committee reported ... that one child named Margaret Jane Alcorn had been admitted. Her mother was dead, and her father and step-mother were supposed to be in the House of Correction. The little girl had been found in a very destitute condition in Carney Place, and had been recommended for admission by Mr. Eustis, one of the Overseers of the Poor. Voted: That the act of the Committee in admitting Margaret Jane Alcorn is sanctioned by the Board.

Name: Margaret Jane Alcorn
entry_text: [annual meeting] One little girl was found last February in a very destitute condition in Carney Place, a neighborhood noted above most of the other by places in our city for its filth and wretchedness. The mother was dead, and the father and step-mother were in the House of Correction. The poor little thing was left with no one to take care of her, and when found was scarely more than half alive, for she could not swallow the improper food which the well meaning neighbors offered her. She brightened up very soon after she was brought here, and a day or two afterwards the ladies who saw her in her wretched abode, could not believe, that the happy looking child who was playing about with the rest could be the miserable little object that they had found so short a time before.

Name: Margaret Jane Alcorn
entry_text: The Committee also stated that a letter had been received from a sister of Margaret Jane Alcorn. She was very comfortably situated in California and very desirous to have her sister with her. She had sent on money for her outfit, and would send the sum necessary to pay her passage. It was decided that Margaret should go to her sister whenever after the receipt of the passage money a suitable opportunity should offer.

Name: Margaret Jane Alcorn
entry_text: The Committee reported ... that the money had been received from Margaret Alcorn's sister to pay the child's passage to California, and that she would soon go under the care of an excellent woman, now living with Mrs. Rea, who was willing to take charge of her.

Name: Margaret Jane Alcorn
entry_text: The Committee also stated that Margaret Alcorn had been fitted out under the superintendence of Mrs. Fearing and that she had gone to California under very good care. 1850 Federal Census, 1st Ward Boston, 536/759 Andrew Alcorn, 33, Laborer, b. Ireland Alice Alcorn, 23, b. Ireland Margaret J., 1, b. MA 1860 Federal Census, 10th Ward Boston, Female Asylum, 209/230 Margaret Allcon, 12
